native_neighbors.definition: A family of nonasymptotic, anytime-valid sequential confidence sequences (Wang & Ramdas 2023, AISTATS / PMLR 206:9662–9679) for the mean mu(P) of an uncorrupted distribution P with bounded variance Var_P(X) <= sigma^2 (or bounded p-th central moment E_P[|X - mu(P)|^p] <= kappa for 1 < p <= 2) when observations X_1, X_2, ... are drawn sequentially from an adversarially contaminated distribution Q in the total-variation neighborhood B_TV(P, varepsilon) = {Q : D_TV(P, Q) <= varepsilon} (strictly generalizing Huber's gross-error contamination model Q = (1 - varepsilon) P + varepsilon N with no moment assumptions on N), constructed by pairing the bounded narrowest Catoni influence function phi(x) in [-log 2, log 2] (where exp(+-phi(x)) lies in [1/2, 2] of range 1.5, or phi_p(x) in [-log p, log p] with exp(+-phi_p(x)) in [1/p, p] of range p - 1/p) with the total-variation integral probability metric shift to form the nonnegative robust Catoni supermartingales M_t^{RC} = prod_{i=1}^t [exp(phi(lambda_i(X_i - mu(P)))) / (1 + lambda_i^2 sigma^2 / 2 + 1.5 varepsilon)] and N_t^{RC} = prod_{i=1}^t [exp(-phi(lambda_i(X_i - mu(P)))) / (1 + lambda_i^2 sigma^2 / 2 + 1.5 varepsilon)], whose Ville inversion CI_t^R = {m in R : |sum_{i=1}^t phi(lambda_i(X_i - m))| <= sum_{i=1}^t log(1 + lambda_i^2 sigma^2 / 2 + 1.5 varepsilon) + log(2/alpha)} under constant tuning lambda = sqrt(varepsilon)/(2 sigma) achieves the minimax-optimal high-probability diameter O(sigma sqrt(varepsilon)) (specifically <= 28 sigma sqrt(varepsilon) for varepsilon <= 1/7 and <= (14 p / (p - 1)) kappa^{1/p} varepsilon^{(p-1)/p} for 1 < p < 2) and non-trivial finite breakdown point varepsilon < 8/13.

native_neighbors.name: Nonparametric two-sample testing by betting
native_neighbors.definition: A general sequential nonparametric two-sample and operator-invariance hypothesis testing framework (Shekhar & Ramdas 2023, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 70(2):1178–1203) that tests H_0 : P_X = P_Y against H_1 : P_X != P_Y from paired streaming observations {(X_t, Y_t) : t >= 1} by exploiting the variational representation of an Integral Probability Metric (IPM) d_G(P_X, P_Y) = sup_{g in G} (E_{P_X}[g(X)] - E_{P_Y}[g(Y)]) over a symmetric bounded witness class G subseteq [-1/2, 1/2]^X to construct an iterative betting game with wealth process K_t = prod_{i=1}^t (1 + lambda_i (g_i(X_i) - g_i(Y_i))), decoupling predictable witness selection g_t in G via a no-regret online learner A_pred (such as adaptive Online Gradient Ascent in Euclidean or reproducing-kernel Hilbert spaces, or empirical risk minimization over low-Rademacher-complexity classes) from predictable bet-fraction selection lambda_t in [-1/2, 1/2] via the Online Newton Step strategy A_ONS, so that stopping at tau = inf{t >= 1 : K_t >= 1/alpha} guarantees nonasymptotic Type-I error P_{H_0}(tau < infty) <= alpha via Ville's inequality alongside variance-adaptive exponential wealth growth, power-one consistency, and minimax-optimal expected stopping time E[tau] = O(sigma^2 log(1/(alpha Delta)) / Delta^2) under H_1.

native_neighbors.name: Sequential kernelized independence testing by betting
native_neighbors.definition: A sequential nonparametric independence hypothesis testing framework (Podkopaev, Blobaum, Kasiviswanathan, & Ramdas 2023, ICML / PMLR 202:27957-27993, arXiv:2212.07383) that tests whether streaming paired random variables Z_t = (X_t, Y_t) on general spaces X x Y are statistically independent (H_0 : P_{XY} = P_X x P_Y against H_1 : P_{XY} != P_X x P_Y) under arbitrary optional stopping and time-varying marginal distributions by pairing consecutive draws (Z_{2t-1}, Z_{2t}) with their coordinate-swapped pseudo-observations tilde{Z}_{2t-1} = (X_{2t-1}, Y_{2t}), tilde{Z}_{2t} = (X_{2t}, Y_{2t-1}) to evaluate predictable witness functions from reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces G x H — instantiated via the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), the Constrained Covariance (COCO), or the Kernel Canonical Correlation (KCC), or via symmetry-preserving odd, sequential signed-rank, and predictive betting payoffs for unbounded kernels — and updating a wealth martingale K_t = prod_{i=1}^t (1 + lambda_i f_i(Z_{2i-1}, Z_{2i})) via the Online Newton Step (ONS) strategy so that stopping at tau = inf{t >= 1 : K_t >= 1/alpha} controls nonasymptotic anytime Type-I error P_{H_0}(tau < infty) <= alpha and achieves power-one consistency with variance-adaptive exponential log-wealth growth.

native_neighbors.name: Reverse-submartingale confidence sequences for convex divergences and functionals
native_neighbors.definition: A sequential nonparametric estimation and inference methodology (Manole & Ramdas 2023, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 69(7):4641-4658, arXiv:2103.09267) that constructs time-uniform confidence sequences for convex functionals Phi(P) of a single distribution and convex divergences Psi(P, Q) between two distributions — including integral probability metrics (Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy, positive-definite V-statistics), optimal transport costs (Wasserstein and Gaussian-smoothed Wasserstein distances), phi-divergences (Kullback-Leibler divergence, Total Variation, and Gaussian-smoothed divergences), classification generalization risks (Rademacher complexity), and general-norm multivariate means — by exploiting the property that empirical measures P_t and Q_s are measure-valued reverse martingales with respect to the exchangeable filtrations (E_t^X)_{t>=1} and (E_s^Y)_{s>=1}, so plug-in estimators Phi(P_t) and Psi(P_t, Q_s) form reverse submartingales (or partially ordered reverse submartingales on N^2) to which Ville's reverse maximal inequality and Christofides-Serfling's partially ordered maximal inequality are stitched across geometric sample-size epochs while affine variational minorants provide matching upper confidence sequences.

native_neighbors.name: Model-X anytime-valid conditional independence testing via e-processes
native_neighbors.definition: A sequential conditional independence testing framework (Grünwald, Henzi, & Lardy 2024, Journal of the American Statistical Association 119(546):1554-1565, arXiv:2209.12637; Shaer, Maman, & Romano 2023, NeurIPS 36, arXiv:2210.00354) for testing H_0: X _||_ Y | Z under the Model-X assumption (where the conditional law Q_{X|Z} is known or estimated while the outcome conditional law P_{Y|X,Z} is completely unspecified) that constructs conditional e-variables E(X_n; Y_n, Z_n) = f(X_n, Y_n, Z_n) / int f(x, Y_n, Z_n) dQ_{X|Z=Z_n}(x) (or exact finite-sample Monte Carlo plus-one approximations E^{(M)}(X_n; Y_n, Z_n) = f(X_n, Y_n, Z_n) / ((1/(M+1))(f(X_n, Y_n, Z_n) + sum_{i=1}^M f(tilde{X}_n^{(i)}, Y_n, Z_n))) using M >= 1 conditional randomization draws tilde{X}_n^{(i)} ~ Q_{X|Z=Z_n}) whose product M_n = prod_{i=1}^n E_i forms a non-negative test martingale under H_0 regardless of the serial dependence of (Y_n, Z_n), achieves Growth-Rate Optimality (GRO) equal to the conditional mutual information I(X; Y | Z) via a conditional Kullback-Leibler divergence regret decomposition, and admits nonasymptotic Total Variation type-I error inflation bounds under Model-X misspecification.

native_neighbors.name: Fork-convex exchangeability testing via universal safe e-processes
native_neighbors.definition: A sequential hypothesis testing and game-theoretic probability framework (Ramdas, Ruf, Larsson, & Koolen 2022, International Journal of Approximate Reasoning 141:83-109, arXiv:2102.00630) for testing whether an observed data stream X_1, X_2, ... is exchangeable (H_0: bar{Q} = convex hull of i.i.d. distributions Q = {Ber(p)^infty : p in [0, 1]} in the canonical filtration (F_t)_{t>=1}) that proves every nonnegative supermartingale (NSM) under Q remains an NSM under the closed fork-convex hull tilde{Q} (which for exchangeable binary laws equals the set of all probability measures on {0, 1}^infty, rendering every canonical-filtration Q-NSM pathwise nonincreasing and powerless), characterizes when a Q-safe e-process E_t satisfying sup_{Q in bar{Q}, tau} E_Q[E_tau] <= 1 is dominated by a Q-NSM via the composite Q-Snell envelope under fork-convexity, and constructs powerful bar{Q}-safe e-processes R_t = inf_{p in [0, 1]} R_t^{JP, p} by dividing k-th order Markov Jeffreys'-prior (Krichevsky-Trofimov) mixtures, countable context-tree double mixtures, or predictable non-anticipating betting likelihoods by the composite i.i.d. maximum likelihood sup_p L_p(X^t).

native_neighbors.name: Simultaneous pathwise false discovery proportion bounds
native_neighbors.definition: A finite-sample multiple-testing and selective-inference methodology (Katsevich & Ramdas 2020, The Annals of Statistics 48(6):3465-3487, arXiv:1803.06790) that constructs simultaneously valid level-(1 - alpha) upper confidence envelopes on the false discovery proportion FDP(R_k) = V(R_k) / max(1, |R_k|) across an entire nested sequence of candidate rejection sets emptyset = R_0 subset R_1 subset ... subset R_m ordered by sorted p-values, covariate-assisted interactive unmasking (STAR/AdaPT), knockoff feature-importance statistics, or online hypothesis streams. By proving a unifying finite-sample exponential supermartingale and empirical-process inequality (Lemma 1 and Lemma 2) to obtain pathwise false-discovery upper bounds V(R_k) <= bar{V}(R_k) and applying closed-testing interpolation tilde{V}(R_k) = min_{0 <= j <= k} {bar{V}(R_j) + |R_k \ R_j|} (Proposition 1), the procedure allows analysts to inspect the entire size-versus-FDP trade-off curve and select any rejection set R_k or target FDP level post hoc without violating simultaneous coverage.

native_neighbors.name: Conditional calibration for false discovery rate control under dependence
native_neighbors.definition: A finite-sample multiple-testing methodology (Fithian & Lei 2022, The Annals of Statistics 50(6):3091-3118, arXiv:2007.10438) that controls the false discovery rate (FDR) under known or conditionals-characterized dependence among test statistics by decomposing FDR into m additive per-hypothesis contributions FDR_i(R) = E[V_i / max(1, |R|)] and calibrating each hypothesis H_i's rejection threshold conditionally on a tailored sufficient conditioning statistic S_i that governs how H_i's test statistic T_i affects all other hypotheses' rejection decisions. Using conditional threshold calibration (Step 1), effective rejection-size bounds R_+^{(i)}(T) >= |R(T)| on V_i = 1 coupled with independent uniform randomized pruning U ~ Unif(0, 1) (Steps 2-3), the general three-step framework (Theorem 1) guarantees exact finite-sample FDR <= alpha m_0 / m <= alpha without union-bound or Benjamini-Yekutieli log-factor conservatism, and yields the dependency-adjusted Benjamini-Hochberg (dBH) and Benjamini-Yekutieli (dBY) procedures (Section 3, Theorem 2) as well as recursive multi-step threshold refinement (Section 4.3, Theorem 3).

native_neighbors.name: Selectively traversed accumulation rules for structured false discovery rate control
native_neighbors.definition: An interactive multiple-testing methodology (Lei, Ramdas, & Fithian 2021, Biometrika 108(2):253-267, arXiv:1710.02776) that controls the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples while enforcing arbitrary structural constraints R_t in K on the discovery set (including rooted tree heredity, directed acyclic graph heredity, spatial convexity or connectedness, and polynomially sized group structures). Given a bounded non-decreasing accumulation function h : [0, 1] -> [0, infinity) satisfying int_0^1 h(p) dp = 1, STAR constructs a paired continuous strictly decreasing reflection s : [0, 1] -> [0, 1] via H(s(p)) = H(p) where H(x) = int_0^x (h(p) - 1) dp, and reveals to the analyst only the masked p-values g(p_i) = min{p_i, s(p_i)} together with side information x_i, the unmasked p-values (p_i)_{i notin R_t} outside the current candidate set R_t, and the aggregate false discovery proportion estimate FDP_hat_t = (h(1) + sum_{i in R_t} h(p_i)) / (1 + |R_t|). Starting from R_0 = [n], the analyst iteratively peels R_{t+1} subsetneq R_t inside K using any F_t-measurable model-assisted or human-in-the-loop rule until tau = inf{t : FDP_hat_t <= alpha}, guaranteeing exact finite-sample conditional FDR control E[FDP(R_tau) | (x_i, g(p_i))_{i=1}^n] <= alpha via optional stopping (Theorem 2.3).

native_neighbors.name: Covariate-powered cross-weighted multiple testing
native_neighbors.definition: A covariate-assisted multiple-testing methodology (Ignatiadis & Huber 2021, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 83(4):720-751, arXiv:1701.05179) that learns data-driven hypothesis weights W_i >= 0 from side information X_i via K-fold sample splitting across hypotheses (cross-weighting) to maximize discovery power while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) or k-familywise error rate (k-FWER). Hypotheses [m] are partitioned into K disjoint folds I_1, ..., I_K; for each i in I_ell, an out-of-fold weight function W_hat^{-ell} is fit using only (P_j, X_j)_{j notin I_ell}, evaluated at X_i, and normalized within fold I_ell so that sum_{i in I_ell} W_i = |I_ell| (Specification 1, honest weighting). Combined with tau-censoring (Specification 2, where weights depend on out-of-fold p-values only through P_j * 1{P_j > tau}) and weighted Storey fold null-proportion adjustments, cross-weighting guarantees finite-sample FDR control under independence (Theorems 1-2), asymptotic FDR control without tau-censoring and zero asymptotic power loss from fold splitting under the conditional two-groups model (Proposition 1, Corollary 2), and finite-sample k-FWER and Benjamini-Yekutieli FDR control under block dependence when folds align with independent dependence blocks (Theorems 3-4).

native_neighbors.name: Adaptive data-driven optimal p-value weighting
native_neighbors.definition: An adaptive grouped multiple-testing methodology (Durand 2019, Electronic Journal of Statistics 13(2):3336-3385, arXiv:1710.01094) that generalizes the Weighted Benjamini-Hochberg (WBH) procedure to Multi-Weighted Benjamini-Hochberg (MWBH) with threshold-dependent weight functions W : [0, 1] -> [0, infinity)^G and constructs Adaptive Data-Driven Optimal Weighting (ADDOW) to simultaneously estimate group null proportions pi_{g,0} and group p-value cumulative distribution functions D_g via their Grenander least concave majorant (LCM) D_tilde_g. At each candidate rejection fraction u in {0, 1/m, ..., 1}, ADDOW solves the constrained maximization W_hat^*(u) in argmax_{w in K_hat} G_hat_w(u) over the null-proportion-adaptive weight budget K_hat = {w in [0, infinity)^G : sum_{g=1}^G (m_g / m) pi_hat_{g,0} w_g <= 1}, where G_hat_w(u) = sum_{g=1}^G (m_g / m) D_hat_g(alpha u w_g), and rejects hypotheses with p_{g,i} <= alpha u_hat_{W_hat^*} W_hat^*_g(u_hat_{W_hat^*}) at the step-up threshold u_hat_{W_hat^*} = max{u in {0, 1/m, ..., 1} : G_hat_{W_hat^*}(u) >= u}. Under Multiplicative Estimation (ME, pi_hat_{g,0} -> C pi_{g,0} with C >= 1), ADDOW controls the false discovery rate asymptotically at alpha / C <= alpha (Theorem 5.1) while achieving the maximum asymptotic discovery power among all WBH and MWBH procedures constrained to K_hat (Theorem 5.2, Corollaries 5.2-5.3), and admits an F-fold cross-weighted stabilization (crADDOW, Section 7, Theorem 7.1) that eliminates finite-sample weak-signal overfitting while preserving full asymptotic power.

native_neighbors.name: Optimal multi-weighted step-up procedure for false discovery rate control
native_neighbors.definition: A step-wise multiple hypothesis testing methodology (Roquain & van de Wiel 2009, Electronic Journal of Statistics 3:678-711, arXiv:0807.4081v3, DOI:10.1214/09-EJS430) that generalizes the weighted Benjamini-Hochberg linear step-up procedure LSU(w) by replacing a single static weight vector w = (w_1, ..., w_m) with a rejection-proportion-indexed weight function W(u) = (W_i(u))_{i=1}^m defined across all candidate rejection proportions u in {1/m, 2/m, ..., 1} subject to budget conservation sum_{i=1}^m W_i(u) = m and threshold monotonicity Delta_i(u) = alpha u W_i(u) non-decreasing in u. Because the optimal static weight vector maximizing expected discovery power Pow_w(u) = m^{-1} sum_{i in H_1} F_i(alpha w_i u) depends on the unknown rejection proportion u = |R|/m, Roquain & van de Wiel (2009) solve the constrained Lagrangian maximization simultaneously at every u in (0, 1], yielding the unique optimal weight function W_i^*(u) = (alpha u)^{-1} f_i^{-1}(y^*(u)) under strictly concave alternative CDFs F_i with densities f_i = F_i', where y^*(u) is chosen so that sum_{i=1}^m W_i^*(u) = m (reducing in the one-sided Gaussian model F_i(x) = Phi_bar(Phi_bar^{-1}(x) - mu_i) to alpha u W_i^*(u) = Phi_bar(mu_i / 2 + c(u) / mu_i), Proposition 3.2, Eq. 11). The multi-weighted step-up procedure SU(W) rejects {i : p_i <= alpha u_hat W_i(u_hat)} at u_hat = max{u in {0, 1/m, ..., 1} : G_hat_W(u) >= u}, while the damped procedures SU(W_tilde) with W_tilde_i(u) = W_i(u) / (1 + alpha W_i(1)) and SD(W_tilde) with W_tilde_i(u) = W_i(u) / (1 + alpha u W_i(u)) guarantee exact finite-sample FDR control <= m_0 alpha / m <= alpha under arbitrary deterministic weight functions or misspecified prior parameters (Theorem 4.1), and unmodified SU(W^*) achieves asymptotic FDR = pi_0 alpha and asymptotic power at least as large as every static weighted linear step-up procedure LSU(w) (Theorems 4.2-4.3).

native_neighbors.name: Bayes optimal p-value weighting under a Gaussian prior on the effect sizes
native_neighbors.definition: A frequentist multiple hypothesis testing p-value weighting methodology (and informed genome-wide association study procedure, iGWAS) introduced by Dobriban, Fortney, Kim, & Owen (2015, Biometrika 102(4):753-766, arXiv:1504.02935v1, DOI:10.1093/biomet/asv050) for testing J one-sided Gaussian mean hypotheses H_i: mu_i >= 0 against mu_i < 0 using test statistics T_i | mu_i ~ N(mu_i, 1) and one-sided p-values P_i = Phi(T_i) at per-test significance level q in [0, 1] (controlling the per-family and family-wise error rates strongly at alpha = J q, or false discovery rate via weighted Benjamini-Hochberg) when prior effect-size information is uncertain and modeled by independent Gaussian priors mu_i ~ N(eta_i, sigma_i^2). Whereas classical Spjotvoll p-value weighting (Spjotvoll 1972; Wasserman & Roeder 2006; Roeder & Wasserman 2009; Rubin et al. 2006) assumes exact known effect sizes (sigma_i = 0) and maximizes a strictly concave objective, positive prior variance sigma_i > 0 induces marginal test statistics T_i ~ N(eta_i, gamma_i^2) with gamma_i = sqrt(sigma_i^2 + 1) > 1, rendering the marginal expected discovery objective sum_{i=1}^J Phi((Phi^{-1}(q w_i) - eta_i) / gamma_i) over w_i in [0, 1/q], sum_{i=1}^J w_i = J non-concave (each summand has a concave interval followed by a convex interval). Despite this non-concavity, whenever q satisfies the mild small-q condition sum_{i=1}^J Phi(c_1(eta_i, gamma_i; 1)) >= J q (Condition 5, Proposition 3.4), the exact global Bayes optimal weights take the closed form w_i = Phi(c_1(eta_i, gamma_i; lambda)) / q where c_1(eta_i, gamma_i; lambda) = (-eta_i - gamma_i sqrt(eta_i^2 + 2(gamma_i^2 - 1) log(gamma_i lambda))) / (gamma_i^2 - 1) and lambda >= 1 is the unique dual multiplier found in O(J) cost per Newton step (Theorem 3.2), recovering the Spjotvoll weights Phi(eta_i / 2 + log(lambda) / eta_i) / q as sigma_i -> 0+ (Proposition 3.3); for general q in [0, 1] when lambda in (0, 1), sorting the unique jump-discontinuity thresholds k_i = k(eta_i, gamma_i) in [l(eta_i, gamma_i), 1] where each summand's global maximum jumps from c_1(eta_i, gamma_i; k_i) to +infinity (weight 1/q) solves the non-convex problem in O(J log J) steps for a nearby level q* with |q* - q| <= 1/(2J) (Theorem 3.5).

native_neighbors.name: Constrained convex p-value weighting in monotone likelihood ratio families (Princessp)
native_neighbors.definition: A convex-optimization p-value weighting methodology (Princessp: 'PRior-INformed, Convexly Constrained Spjotvoll') introduced by Edgar Dobriban (2018, Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA 7(2):251-275, arXiv:1603.05334v2, DOI:10.1093/imaiai/iax013) for testing massive collections of J hypotheses H_{0,j}: theta_j = theta_{0,j} against H_{a,j}: theta_j = theta_{a,j} at per-test significance level q in (0, 1) using p-values P_j and prior weights w_j >= 0 with J^{-1} sum_{j=1}^J w_j = 1 (controlling the family-wise error rate via weighted Bonferroni P_j <= q w_j or the false discovery rate via weighted Benjamini-Hochberg). By re-parametrizing the power of the j-th test in terms of the p-value threshold u_j = q w_j as the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) function R_j(u_j) = F_{a,j}(F_{0,j}^{-1}(u_j)) rather than the non-concave critical-value parametrization c_j = F_{0,j}^{-1}(q w_j), Dobriban proves that R_j(u_j) is concave on [0, 1] whenever the test statistic comes from an absolutely continuous parametric family with monotone likelihood ratio (MLR) for one-sided tests (Proposition 2.1) or from a canonical exponential family for two-sided equal-tailed tests |T_j| >= z(u_j/2) (Proposition 2.2), where unconstrained two-sided Gaussian weights take the closed form w_j^* = 2 q^{-1} Phi(-|mu_j|/2 - |mu_j|^{-1} arccosh(lambda exp(mu_j^2/2))) (Proposition 2.3). Because unconstrained Spjotvoll weights become non-monotone in |mu_j| when q exceeds a critical level (assigning less weight to the largest effect sizes; Propositions 3.1-3.2) and place zero weight on small prior effects, Princessp maximizes J^{-1} sum_{j=1}^J R_j(q w_j) subject to the convex constraint set C = {w in R^J : J^{-1} sum_{j=1}^J w_j = 1, l <= w_j <= u, w_1 <= w_2 <= ... <= w_J} for hypotheses sorted by increasing |mu_j|, enforcing effect-size monotonicity and non-zero minimum weights l in (0, 1] via an O(J)-step interior-point Newton solver whose barrier Hessian + order-constraint KKT matrix reduces to a symmetric tridiagonal-plus-rank-1 system solved in O(J) time via the Sherman-Morrison formula combined with hybrid subsampling for large J.

native_neighbors.name: Optimal Spjøtvoll and sieve-grouped p-value weighting
native_neighbors.definition: A frequentist family-wise error rate (FWER) p-value weighting and robustness framework developed by Kathryn Roeder and Larry Wasserman (2009, Statistical Science 24(4):398-413, arXiv:1010.4637v1, DOI:10.1214/09-STS289) for testing m hypotheses H_j: xi_j = 0 versus xi_j > 0 with standardized statistics T_j ~ N(xi_j, 1) and one-sided p-values P_j = Phi_bar(T_j), rejecting H_j when P_j <= alpha w_j / m (equivalently T_j > z_{alpha w_j / m}) for weights w_j >= 0 satisfying m^{-1} sum_{j=1}^m w_j = 1 (Lemma 2.1) or E_H[W_j] <= 1 for random auxiliary weights W_j = g(V_j, c) independent of P_j under H_j (Lemma 2.2). Maximizing average power m_1^{-1} sum_{j: xi_j > 0} Phi_bar(z_{alpha w_j / m} - xi_j) yields the one-parameter Spjøtvoll/Rubin-Dudoit-van der Laan oracle weight family w_j = rho_c(xi_j) = (m/alpha) Phi_bar(xi_j/2 + c/xi_j) for xi_j > 0 (and 0 for xi_j = 0), where c = c(theta) solves m^{-1} sum_{j=1}^m rho_c(xi_j) = 1 and gives test-specific critical cutoffs T_j > xi_j/2 + c/xi_j and oracle power Phi_bar(c/xi_j - xi_j/2) (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2). Roeder and Wasserman prove two fundamental robustness properties explaining why poorly specified weights still outperform unweighted Bonferroni: (Property I) for worst-case binary weights B = min{w_j : w_j > 1} and b = min{w_j}, the robustness function (power gain minus power loss) R(xi) = [pi(xi, B) - pi(xi, 1)] - [pi(xi, 1) - pi(xi, b)] is positive iff Phi_bar(z_{B alpha/m} - xi) + Phi_bar(z_{b alpha/m} - xi) > 2 Phi_bar(z_{alpha/m} - xi) (Theorem 3.4) and remains positive on a non-empty safe zone [0, xi_*] even when b = 0 and B >= 2 (Lemma 3.5); and (Property II) although the optimal weight functional Q -> rho_Q(xi) is discontinuous in Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance d(Q, Q_tilde) = gamma when a fraction gamma of nulls are misspecified as positive mean u > 0 (Lemma 3.6), the worst-case power inf_{u >= 0} pi_u(xi) occurs at the least-favorable false-positive mean u_* = sqrt(2 c_*) solving gamma Phi_bar(sqrt(2 c_*)) + a Phi_bar(xi/2 + c_*/xi) = alpha/m and equals Phi_bar(c_*/xi - xi/2), which still beats unweighted Bonferroni for xi < xi_* and has asymptotic power deficit bounded by gamma/(1 - a) + O(a) (Theorems 3.7-3.8). To construct practical weights, the method provides both closed-form maximin binary external weights (Theorems 4.1-4.3) and a sieve-principle data-driven grouped estimator that partitions tests into K << m prior groups G_k of size r_k >= 20-30, estimates group mixture parameters (pi_k, xi_k) under T_{ik} ~ (1 - pi_k) N(0, 1) + pi_k N(xi_k, 1) via method of moments pi_hat_k = Y_k^2 / (Y_k^2 + S_k^2 - 1) and xi_hat_k = Y_k / pi_hat_k (Equation 12; or Equation 13 for two-sided chi_1^2 mixtures), and forms linearly smoothed group weights w_hat_k = (1 - gamma) w(xi_hat_k) + gamma K^{-1} sum_{k'} w(xi_hat_{k'}) with gamma in {0.01, 0.05} (Section 5).

native_neighbors.name: Self-consistency and dependency control framework for false discovery rate control
native_neighbors.definition: A modular mathematical framework for multiple hypothesis testing on any countable (or continuous) hypothesis space H equipped with a finite positive volume measure Lambda and factorized threshold collection Delta(h, r) = alpha pi(h) beta(r) (with p-value weight density pi: H -> [0, 1] and nondecreasing shape function beta: R^+ -> R^+) developed by Gilles Blanchard and Etienne Roquain (2008, Electronic Journal of Statistics 2:963-992, arXiv:0802.1406v2, DOI:10.1214/08-EJS180) that decouples control of the Lambda-weighted False Discovery Rate FDR(R) = E[(Lambda(R cap H_0) / Lambda(R)) 1{Lambda(R) > 0}] into two sufficient conditions: (1) the geometric Self-Consistency Condition SC(alpha, pi, beta), requiring R subset L_Delta(|R|) almost surely where |R| = Lambda(R) and L_Delta(r) = {h in H : p_h <= Delta(h, r)}, and (2) the probabilistic Dependency Control Condition DC(beta), requiring E[1{p_h <= c beta(|R|)} / |R|] <= c for every true null h in H_0 and c > 0, which together imply FDR(R) <= alpha Pi(H_0) = alpha sum_{h in H_0} Lambda({h}) pi(h) across independence, positive regression dependency (PRDS), and arbitrary dependence via the prior-integrated shape function family beta_nu(r) = int_0^r x d_nu(x).

native_neighbors.name: One-stage and two-stage adaptive step-up procedures for false discovery rate control under independence and dependence
native_neighbors.definition: A family of one-stage and two-stage adaptive multiple hypothesis testing procedures developed by Gilles Blanchard and Etienne Roquain (2009, Journal of Machine Learning Research 10:2837-2871, arXiv:0707.0536v3) that adapt step-up thresholds to the unknown null proportion pi_0 = m_0 / m while controlling the finite-sample False Discovery Rate under independent, positively dependent (PRDS), or arbitrarily dependent p-values: (1) the one-stage piecewise inverse-volume procedure BR-1S-lambda with threshold collection Delta(i) = min(lambda, alpha (1 - lambda) i / (m - i + 1)) (default lambda = alpha), which modifies the asymptotically optimal Finner-Dickhaus-Roters rejection curve to guarantee exact finite-sample FDR <= alpha for any coordinate-wise non-increasing self-consistent procedure under independence (Theorem 3.1); (2) the two-stage plug-in procedure BR-2S-lambda using estimator G_4(p) = (1 - lambda) m / (m - |R_{BR-1S-lambda}(p)| + 1), which dominates the Benjamini-Krieger-Yekutieli (2006) estimator G_3 while satisfying the unified self-consistent plug-in bound FDR(R) <= (alpha / m) sum_{h in H_0} E[G(p_{0,h})] <= alpha under independence (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 1); (3) the tuning principle lambda = alpha that prevents catastrophic FDR inflation under comonotonic/strong positive dependence (Proposition 1); and (4) two-stage adaptive step-up procedures for PRDS and arbitrary dependence using either an FWER-controlled first stage Delta(i) = alpha_1 (m - |R_0|)^{-1} beta(i) (Theorem 4.1) or an FDR-controlled first stage with the Markov-inequality transformation F_kappa(x) = 2 / (kappa - sqrt((kappa^2 - 4 kappa (1 - x))_+)) for x >= 1/kappa (Theorem 4.2).

native_neighbors.name: Measure-theoretic step-up false discovery rate control over a continuum of null hypotheses
native_neighbors.definition: A measure-theoretic multiple hypothesis testing framework developed by Gilles Blanchard, Sylvain Delattre, and Etienne Roquain (2014, Bernoulli 20(1):304-333, arXiv:1110.3599v3, DOI:10.3150/12-BEJ488) that extends step-up False Discovery Rate control to an arbitrary (possibly uncountably infinite) measurable index space of hypotheses (H, frak_H, Lambda) with finite positive measure Lambda(H) < infty: given a measurable p-value process (p_h(X))_{h in H} and threshold collection Delta(h, r) = alpha pi(h) beta(r), the continuum step-up procedure rejects R_{SU}(X) = L_Delta(r_hat(X)) where L_Delta(r) = {h in H : p_h(X) <= Delta(h, r)} and r_hat(X) = max{r in [0, Lambda(H)] : Lambda(L_Delta(r)) >= r} (satisfying the exact fixed-point volume identity Lambda(L_Delta(r_hat(X))) = r_hat(X) when Delta is left-continuous in r), and controls FDR(R_{SU}) = E[(Lambda(R_{SU} cap H_0) / Lambda(R_{SU})) 1{Lambda(R_{SU}) > 0}] <= alpha int_{H_0} pi d_Lambda either (1) under linear shape beta(r) = r when the p-value process is weakly Positive Regression Dependent on a Subset (weakly PRDS on H_0, meaning all finite marginals (p_h)_{h in F} are PRDS on F cap H_0; Definition 2.4 and Theorem 4.1) via Glivenko-Cantelli empirical measure approximations Lambda_n -> Lambda (Section 5.1, Lemmas 5.1-5.3), or (2) under arbitrary dependence with prior-integrated shape beta_nu(r) = int_0^r u d_nu(u).

native_neighbors.name: Step-up-down least favorable configuration and two-population Steck false discovery rate bounds
native_neighbors.definition: A finite-sample and non-asymptotic statistical multiple-testing framework developed by Gilles Blanchard, Thorsten Dickhaus, Etienne Roquain, and Fanny Villers (2014, Statistica Sinica 24(1):1-23, arXiv:1108.5262v1, DOI:10.5705/ss.2011.205) that evaluates and bounds the False Discovery Rate (FDR) of step-up-down procedures SUD_lambda(t) of order lambda in {1, ..., m} under two-group fixed-mixture FM(m, m_0, F) and random-mixture RM(m, pi_0, F) independent p-value models: (1) generalizes Steck's order-statistic recursion to two heterogeneous populations (k_0 uniform true nulls and k - k_0 alternatives with c.d.f. F; Proposition 5.1, Equation (18)) to compute exact finite-sample joint (V, R) distributions and exact FDR(SUD_lambda(t)) (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3); (2) disproves the conjecture (Conjecture 3.2) that the Dirac-uniform configuration (F == 1) is a universal finite-sample least favorable configuration (LFC) for intermediate linear step-up-down procedures LSUD_lambda (Proposition 4.1); and (3) brackets the discrete rejection fraction hat_k/m via the continuous fixed-point functional U(ell, G) (Definition 4.2, Lemma 4.3) to prove explicit Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz perturbation bounds (Theorem 4.4) and O((1 - zeta_m)^{-1} sqrt((log m) / m)) convergence rates (Corollary 4.5) quantifying the maximum excess of FDR(SUD_lambda(t), F) over FDR(SUD_lambda(t), F == 1) for both Simes linear and Finner-Dickhaus-Roters asymptotically optimal rejection curves (AORC).

native_neighbors.name: Archimedean copula linear step-up false discovery rate bounds and calibration
native_neighbors.definition: A statistical multiple hypothesis testing and False Discovery Rate (FDR) analysis framework developed by Taras Bodnar and Thorsten Dickhaus (2014, Electronic Journal of Statistics 8(2):2207-2241, arXiv:1305.3897v3, DOI:10.1214/14-EJS950) that models joint p-value distributions P = (P_1, ..., P_m)^T under an Archimedean copula F_P(p_1, ..., p_m) = psi(sum_{i=1}^m psi^{-1}(F_{P_i}(p_i))) with a completely monotone generator psi(t) = E[exp(-t*Z)] via the Marshall-Olkin conditionally independent frailty representation P_i = F_{P_i}^{-1}(psi(-log(Y_i)/Z)): (1) derives a sharper finite-sample upper bound FDR_{vartheta,psi}(phi^{LSU}) <= (m_0(vartheta)/m)*q - b(m, vartheta, psi) for the Benjamini-Hochberg linear step-up test phi^{LSU} (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.1) without invoking general MTP_2 inequalities, evaluating the conditional order-statistic probabilities G_k^i(z) under Dirac-uniform configurations via Bolshev's recursion (Equations (26)-(27)); (2) establishes a generator-dependent finite-sample lower bound FDR_{vartheta,psi}(phi^{LSU}) >= (m_0*q/m)*gamma_min(psi) via single-crossing thresholds z^* (Theorem 3.2, Lemma 3.1, Corollary 3.2) with a closed-form incomplete-gamma expression for the Clayton copula (Equations (24)-(25)); (3) characterizes infinite H_0-exchangeable p-value sequences whose m-dimensional marginals are Archimedean copulae possessing the MTP_2 property (Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.3); and (4) increases the power of phi^{LSU} by pre-estimating the copula parameter eta via pairwise Kendall's tau method-of-moments or maximum likelihood on resampled data and calibrating the nominal level q (Section 5, Equations (34)-(35)).

native_neighbors.name: exact step-up and step-down false discovery proportion moment formulas and least favorable configuration analysis
native_neighbors.definition: A finite-sample multiple hypothesis testing analysis framework developed by Etienne Roquain and Fanny Villers (2011, Annals of Statistics 39(1):584-612, arXiv:1002.2845v2, DOI:10.1214/10-AOS847) that characterizes the exact joint distribution and moments of the False Discovery Proportion (FDP) for general step-up SU(t) and step-down SD(t) procedures under the unconditional independent two-group mixture model P_bar^I_{(pi_0, F_1)} and equicorrelated multivariate normal (EMN) dependence: (1) proves that conditionally on |SU(t)| = k, the number of false rejections |H_0(H) cap SU(t)| is exactly binomial Binom(k, pi_0*F_0(t_k)/G(t_k)) where G(t) = pi_0*F_0(t) + pi_1*F_1(t) (Theorem 3.1, Equation (11)), yielding exact finite-sample formulas for the FDP cumulative distribution function (Equation (12)), all s-th moments E[FDP(SU(t), H)^s] via Stirling numbers of the second kind {s \atop ell} and step-up rejection-count probabilities D_{m-ell} (Equation (13)), the FDR (Equation (14)), and polynomial-time average power (Equation (15)); (2) proves that |H_0(H) cap SD(t)| given |SD(t)| = k is not binomial for general alternatives F_1 (Equations (16)-(18)) and derives the exact joint rejection distribution (Equation (19)), exact step-down FDR formula (Theorem 3.2, Equation (20)), and closed-form Finner-Roters expansion for linear step-down (LSD) in the Dirac-uniform model (Equation (21)); (3) extends exact SU/SD FDP distribution and moment formulas to non-negatively equicorrelated Gaussian models via 1D/2D Gaussian conditioning (Corollaries 3.4-3.5, Proposition 3.6) and constructs a two-hypothesis negatively correlated Gaussian configuration (m = 2, m_0 = 1, rho -> -1^-, mu = z_1 + z_2) where FDR(LSU) = 3*alpha/4 = alpha*(m_0/m)*(1 + 1/2), attaining the full Benjamini-Yekutieli upper bound and disproving the Dirac-uniform LFC conjecture under negative correlation (Section 4.1.2, Equations (25)-(26)); (4) establishes Condition (A) for step-down procedures to have the Dirac-uniform distribution F_1 == 1 as their least favorable configuration over concave alternative c.d.f.s F_1 in F', proving that LSD satisfies Condition (A) (Theorem 4.1, Equation (24)); and (5) derives exact closed-form minimum and maximum of Var[FDP(LSU)] over general and concave alternative classes F, F', and F_eps (Theorem 4.3, Equations (28)-(30)).

native_neighbors.name: asymptotically optimal rejection curve false discovery rate control and adjusted step-up-down testing
native_neighbors.definition: An asymptotic and finite-sample multiple hypothesis testing framework introduced by Helmut Finner, Thorsten Dickhaus, and Markus Roters (2009, Annals of Statistics 37(2):596-618, arXiv:0903.5161v1, DOI:10.1214/07-AOS569) that derives the Asymptotically Optimal Rejection Curve (AORC) f_alpha(t) = t / (t*(1 - alpha) + alpha) for t in [0, 1] with inverse critical value function f_alpha^{-1}(u) = alpha*u / (1 - (1 - alpha)*u) = 1 - f_alpha(1 - u) and induced critical values alpha_{i:n} = i*alpha / (n - i*(1 - alpha)) (Section 3, Equation (3.1), Remark 3.1) by exhausting the False Discovery Rate (FDR) level alpha in (0, 1) across all limiting Dirac-uniform configurations DU_infty(zeta) with limiting empirical c.d.f. F_infty(t | zeta) = (1 - zeta) + zeta*t (zeta in [alpha, 1)). Because alpha_{n:n} = 1 causes an unadjusted step-up procedure based on f_alpha to reject all n hypotheses whenever p_{n:n} < 1, the framework introduces three families of regularized AORC procedures (Examples 3.1-3.3): (1) step-up-down (SUD) procedures phi^lambda of asymptotic order lambda in [0, 1), (2) linearly adjusted step-up procedures based on f^{(1)}_{alpha,kappa} (tangent continuation h_1(x) = f_alpha'(kappa)*(x - kappa) + f_alpha(kappa)) and f^{(2)}_{alpha,kappa} (secant continuation h_2(x) = x*f_alpha(kappa)/kappa), and (3) truncated step-up procedures with critical value curve rho_alpha(x) = min{f_alpha^{-1}(x), kappa}. It establishes general finite-sample FDR upper bounds via conditional rejection-monotonicity conditions (D1)-(D2) and the least isotonic majorant q_bar(x) = max_{0 <= t <= x} rho(t)/t (Section 4, Theorems 4.1-4.3, Equations (4.1)-(4.12)), proves asymptotic FDR control at level alpha with exact limiting FDR formulas at nonzero and zero crossing points r^* (Section 5, Theorems 5.1-5.4, Corollary 5.1, Equations (5.1)-(5.11)), proves that f_alpha is the pointwise minimal rejection curve and maximizes asymptotic power beta_bar_vartheta over the class M_1 of regular asymptotic level-alpha rejection curves (Theorem 5.5, Equations (5.12)-(5.14)), and introduces the finite-sample beta_n-adjusted critical values alpha_{i:n}(beta_n) = i*alpha / (n + beta_n - i*(1 - alpha)) (Section 6, Equation (6.1)).

native_neighbors.name: exchangeable largest crossing point asymptotic false discovery rate and global-null independence limit discontinuity
native_neighbors.definition: An asymptotic multiple hypothesis testing analysis framework introduced by Helmut Finner, Thorsten Dickhaus, and Markus Roters (2007, Annals of Statistics 35(4):1432-1455, arXiv:0710.3171v1, DOI:10.1214/009053607000000046) that characterizes the limiting Expected Error Rate EER_infty(zeta) = lim_{n->infty} E[V_n/n] and limiting False Discovery Rate FDR_infty(zeta) = lim_{n->infty} E[V_n/(R_n vee 1)] of the linear step-up (LSU / Benjamini-Hochberg) procedure with Simes rejection curve r_alpha(t) = t/alpha under exchangeable test statistics T_i = g(X_i, Z) (i = 1, ..., n) generated by i.i.d. innovations X_1, ..., X_n and a common latent disturbance Z in Dirac-exchangeable configurations D-EX(zeta_n) with n_0/n -> zeta in (0, 1]. Conditioning on Z = z makes the p-values conditionally independent with limiting conditional empirical c.d.f. F_infty(t | z, zeta) = (1 - zeta) + zeta*(1 - W_X(g_1(W_T^{-1}(1 - t), z))) (Lemma 2.1, Equation (2.2)) and Largest Crossing Point (LCP) t(z | zeta) = sup{t in [alpha*(1 - zeta), alpha] : F_infty(t | z, zeta) = t/alpha} (Equation (2.3)). For zeta in (0, 1), V_n(z)/n -> t(z | zeta)/alpha - (1 - zeta) a.s. and V_n(z)/(R_n(z) vee 1) -> 1 - alpha*(1 - zeta)/t(z | zeta) a.s. (Theorems 2.1-2.2, Equations (2.4)-(2.9)). At the complete null zeta = 1 where t(z | 1) = 0 on E_0, Lemma 2.2 and Theorems 2.3-2.4 prove that FDR_infty(1 | z) = alpha*gamma(z) with right-hand derivative gamma(z) = lim_{t->0^+} F_infty(t | z)/t and FDR_infty(1) = P^Z(E_1) + alpha * int_{E_0} gamma(z) dP^Z(z) (Equations (2.10)-(2.15)). Applying this theory to equicorrelated normal variables D-EX-N(zeta_n) (Section 3, Theorems 3.1-3.3, Remark 3.1, Equations (3.1)-(3.6)) and jointly studentized normal variables D-EX-t(zeta_n) (Section 4, Lemma 4.1, Theorems 4.1-4.3, Equation (4.1)) proves that at zeta = 1, gamma(z) == 0 on E_0, and as the correlation rho -> 0^+ or degrees of freedom nu -> infty, lim_{rho->0^+} FDR_infty(1) = lim_{nu->infty} FDR_infty(1) = Phi(-sqrt(-2*ln(alpha))) < alpha for all alpha in (0, 1/2], demonstrating a strict non-commutativity of the sample-size limit n -> infty and the independence limit (rho -> 0^+ or nu -> infty) at the global null.

native_neighbors.name: Hadamard-differentiable threshold functional false discovery proportion central limit theorems and adaptive fixed-point iteration duality
native_neighbors.definition: An asymptotic empirical-process and functional Delta-method framework introduced by Pierre Neuvial (2008, Electronic Journal of Statistics 2:1065-1110, arXiv:0803.2111v2, DOI:10.1214/08-EJS207) that characterizes the limiting distribution of the random rejection threshold T(G_hat_m) and the achieved False Discovery Proportion FDP_m(T(G_hat_m)) = V(G_hat_{0,m}, G_hat_{1,m}) / (R(pi_0*G_hat_{0,m} + (1 - pi_0)*G_hat_{1,m}) vee (1/m)) of multiple testing procedures under independent p-values. Representing any threshold procedure on cadlag distribution functions D[0, 1] as T(F) = U(F, A(F)) with U(F, alpha) = sup{u in [0, 1] : F(u) >= r_alpha(u)}, rejection curve r_alpha, and level function A : D[0, 1] -> [0, 1] (Definitions 2.1-2.2, Section 2.2), Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 7.13 prove that when T has a unique interior right crossing point tau^* = T(G) in (0, 1) where G(tau^*) = r(A(G), tau^*) and g(tau^*) < d_u r(A(G), tau^*) (Definition 3.7, Conditions C.1-C.3), T is Hadamard-differentiable at G tangentially to C[0, 1] with derivative T_dot_G(H) = (H(tau^*) - d_alpha r(A(G), tau^*)*A_dot_G(H)) / (d_u r(A(G), tau^*) - g(tau^*)) (Proposition 7.11, Corollary 7.12), and sqrt(m)*(FDP_m(T(G_hat_m)) - p(tau^*)) converges in distribution to the centered Gaussian limit X = p^*(1 - p^*)*(Z_0(tau^*)/tau^* - Z_1(tau^*)/G_1(tau^*)) + p_dot(tau^*)*T_dot_G(Z), while o(m^{-1/2}) threshold perturbations are asymptotically equivalent (Definition 3.5, Proposition 3.6). Applying this theorem yields explicit Central Limit Theorems and asymptotic power comparisons for BH95, BH95 Oracle, one-stage adaptive procedures FDR08(lambda) and BR08(lambda), and two-stage plug-in procedures Sto02(lambda)/STS04(lambda) and BKY06(lambda) (Section 4, Theorems 4.2, 4.7, 4.10, 4.12, 4.15, Corollary 4.16, Theorem 4.20, Table 1), and establishes a formal fixed-point iteration duality proving that the asymptotic threshold of the one-stage procedure FDR08 is the fixed point of iterating the two-stage procedure Sto02(lambda) and the asymptotic threshold of BR08(lambda) is the fixed point of iterating BKY06(lambda) (Section 5, Theorems 5.2, 5.4, 5.6, Corollaries 5.3, 5.5, 5.7).

native_neighbors.name: Reference-family joint error rate post hoc confidence bounds
native_neighbors.definition: A user-agnostic post hoc multiple-testing and selective-inference framework introduced by Gilles Blanchard, Pierre Neuvial, and Etienne Roquain (2020, The Annals of Statistics 48(3):1281-1303, arXiv:1703.02307v3/v2, DOI:10.1214/19-AOS1847) that constructs simultaneous level-(1 - alpha) upper confidence bounds V(R) on the number of false positives |R cap H_0(P)| (and complementary lower bounds S(R) = |R| - V(R) on true discoveries |R cap H_1(P)|) valid uniformly over all 2^m candidate subsets R subset N_m = {1, ..., m}. Given a reference family R_ref = (R_k(X), zeta_k(X))_{1 <= k <= K} with controlled Joint Family-Wise Error Rate JER(R_ref, P) = 1 - P_{X~P}(forall k in {1, ..., K}, |R_k(X) cap H_0(P)| <= zeta_k(X)) <= alpha, the framework interpolates from R_ref to arbitrary user-selected sets R via both the worst-case optimal bound V^*_{R_ref}(R) = max_{A in A(R_ref)} |R cap A| and the polynomial-time bound V_bar_{R_ref}(R) = min_{1 <= k <= K} (|R \ R_k| + zeta_k) wedge |R|, proving exact event equivalence E(R_ref, H_0) = {forall R subset N_m, |R cap H_0| <= V_bar_{R_ref}(R)} = {forall R subset N_m, |R cap H_0| <= V^*_{R_ref}(R)} (Proposition 2.1), NP-hardness of V^*_{R_ref}(R) in general (Proposition 2.3), self-consistency idempotence V_bar_{tilde{R_ref}}(R) = V_bar_{R_ref}(R) (Proposition 2.4), and exact optimality V_bar_{R_ref}(R) = V^*_{R_ref}(R) whenever the reference regions R_1 subset ... subset R_K are nested (Proposition 2.5), while calibrating p-value threshold templates t_k(lambda) (linear t_k^L(lambda) = lambda k/m and balanced Beta-quantile t_k^B(lambda) = F_k^{-1}(lambda)) via single-step lambda(alpha, N_m) and step-down Algorithm 1 lambda(alpha, A_hat) under known dependence (LeastFavor, Theorem 5.7) or unknown dependence via finite transformation groups (Rand, Theorem 5.8).

native_neighbors.name: Forest-structured Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz post hoc confidence bounds
native_neighbors.definition: A multiple-testing post hoc inference methodology that constructs simultaneous (1 - alpha)-confidence upper bounds V(S) on the number of false positives |S cap H_0(P)| across all 2^m subsets S subset N_m = {1, ..., m} by combining a deterministic forest-structured reference family R_ref = (R_k, zeta_k(X))_{k in K} (where any two regions R_k, R_{k'} are either disjoint or nested: R_k cap R_{k'} in {R_k, R_{k'}, empty}) with random local Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz-Massart (DKW) upper bounds zeta_k(X). Unlike nested data-dependent p-value level-set reference families with fixed capacities zeta_k = k - 1, multi-subset interpolation V_tilde^q_{R_ref}(S) = min_{Q subset K, |Q| <= q} (sum_{k in Q} (zeta_k wedge |S cap R_k|) + |S \ cup_{k in Q} R_k|) is proven to equal the exact combinatorial optimal bound V^*_{R_ref}(S) = V_tilde_{R_ref}(S) = V_tilde^d_{R_ref}(S) whenever R_ref has a forest structure (where d is the maximum number of pairwise disjoint regions in R_ref, Theorem 3.6) and is computable in O(Hm) (or bilinear O(|K| |S|)) time via a bottom-up tree dynamic program over the completed atomic forest R_ref^oplus (Algorithm 1). Local capacities calibrated via quadratic inversion of the tight Massart-DKW inequality control the Joint Error Rate at level alpha under null super-uniformity and independence (Proposition 4.1), uniformly dominate the Genovese-Wasserman (2004) DKW bound (Remark 4.3, Lemma A.1), improve Simes and Bonferroni post hoc bounds by an asymptotic factor 1 - r on localized signal regions of signal density r (Proposition 4.5, Corollary 4.6), and combine with the Simes bound into a hybrid envelope V^gamma_{hybrid}(alpha, S) = min(V_{Simes}((1-gamma)alpha, S), V_{tree}(gamma*alpha, S)) (Section 5.3).

native_neighbors.name: Simes closed-testing concentration-set shortcut and double-asymptotic false discovery proportion consistency
native_neighbors.definition: Simes closed-testing concentration-set shortcut and double-asymptotic false discovery proportion (FDP) consistency is the multiple-testing methodology introduced by Goeman, Meijer, Krebs, and Solari (2019) for closed testing (Marcus, Peritz, & Gabriel 1976; Goeman & Solari 2011) with Simes local tests I in U_alpha iff min_{1 <= i <= |I|} |I| * p_{(i:I)} / i <= alpha across m hypotheses H_1, ..., H_m with true null index set T subseteq {1, ..., m}. Letting K_i = {r_{m-i+1}, ..., r_m} denote the index set of the i largest p-values and defining Hommel's worst-case non-rejected intersection size h_alpha = max{0 <= i <= m : K_i not in U_alpha} (which yields the simultaneous (1 - alpha)-upper confidence bound pi_hat_alpha = h_alpha / m on |T| / m), the method characterizes closed-testing rejections X_alpha = {I : forall J supseteq I, J in U_alpha} via I in X_alpha iff exists 1 <= i <= |I| such that h_alpha * p_{(i:I)} <= i * alpha (Lemma 2), and establishes the exact all-subset shortcut (Theorem 1) for the simultaneous (1 - alpha)-lower bound d_alpha(S) = |S| - t_alpha(S) on true discoveries |S \ T| and upper bound q_alpha(S) = t_alpha(S) / |S| on the FDP pi(S) = |T cap S| / |S|: d_alpha(S) = max_{1 <= u <= |S|} (1 - u + |{i in S : h_alpha * p_i <= u * alpha}|), where the maximization over u restricts to 1 <= u <= z_alpha - m + h_alpha + 1 with z_alpha = min{m - h_alpha <= i <= m : h_alpha * p_{(i)} <= (i - m + h_alpha + 1) * alpha} for h_alpha < m and 0 for h_alpha = m (Lemma 3), enabling O(|S|) per-subset evaluation after a one-time O(m log m) computation of h_alpha. The concentration set Z_alpha = L_{z_alpha} of the z_alpha smallest p-values is the unique minimal set satisfying d_alpha(S) = d_alpha(S cap Z_alpha) for all S subseteq {1, ..., m}, with d_alpha(Z_alpha) = m - h_alpha and |S cap R_alpha| <= d_alpha(S) <= |S cap Z_alpha| <= |S cap B_alpha| between Hommel's elementary FWER set R_alpha and the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) set B_alpha = L_{b_alpha} (Lemma 4), while alpha * q_alpha(B_q) <= pi_hat_alpha * q holds simultaneously for all q in [0, 1] (Lemma 5). Under Efron's mixture model P_n(x) = gamma * x + (1 - gamma) * P_{1,n}(x), Non-consonant Simes rejections yield non-vanishing average discovery power whenever P_n is Simes-detectable (bar_pi_alpha = inf_{0 <= x < 1} (1 - P_n(x * alpha)) / (1 - x) < 1, Lemma 6 and Theorem 2) even though |R_alpha| / m ->^P 0, and for any subset sequence S_m with plim_{m -> infty} |S_m| / m = c > 0 and consistent alternative tests lim_{n -> infty} P^S_{1,n}(x) = 1, q_{alpha,m,n}(S_m) is a doubly asymptotically consistent estimator of the true subset FDP gamma_S = plim_{m -> infty} pi(S_m) as (m, n) -> infty at arbitrary relative rates for any fixed alpha in (0, 1) (Theorem 3).

native_neighbors.name: Restricted isometry post-selection inference (PoSI) constant upper and lower bounds
native_neighbors.definition: A post-selection inference methodology for linear Gaussian regression Y = mu + epsilon (epsilon ~ N(0, sigma^2 I_n)) that bounds the Berk-Brown-Buja-Zhang-Zhao (2013) Post-Selection Inference (PoSI) constant K(X, M_s, alpha, r)—the (1 - alpha) quantile of the studentized maximum projection statistic gamma_{M_s, r} = (1 / N) max_{M in M_s, i in M} |w_{M, i}^t xi| over all s-sparse submodels M_s = {M subset {1, ..., p} : rank(X_M) = |M| <= s} where w_{M, i} = v_{M, i} / ||v_{M, i}|| and v_{M, i} is the i-th column of X_M (X_M^t X_M)^{-1}—as an explicit function of the correlation-matrix Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) constant delta(X, s) = sup_{M in M_s} ||corr(X_M^t X_M) - I_{|M|}||_op. Because K(X, M, alpha, r) depends on X only through corr(X^t X) (Lemma 2.2) and satisfies the Cirel'son-Ibragimov-Sudakov Gaussian-concentration quantile bound K(X, M, alpha, r) <= T(E[gamma_{M, infty}], r, 1 - alpha/2) (Proposition 2.3), decomposing each dual projection vector w_{M, i} into its normalized column z_{M, i} = X_{M, i} / ||X_{M, i}|| plus a residual of norm at most 2 * delta * c(delta) with c(delta) = sqrt(1 + delta) / (1 - delta) yields the RIP-interpolating Gaussian-width upper bound E[gamma_{M_s, infty}] <= U_RIP(p, s, delta) = sqrt(2 log(2p)) + 2 * delta * c(delta) * sqrt(2 s log(6p / s)) (Theorem 3.3) and the sharper Beta-Fisher quantile union-split bound U_tilde_RIP(p, s, delta) = inf_{t in (0, 1)} {B_{t*alpha}(n wedge p, r, p) + 2 * delta * c(delta) * B_{(1-t)*alpha}(n wedge p, r, |M_s|)} (Section 3.3), smoothly interpolating between the orthogonal-design rate sqrt(2 log(2p)) (delta = 0) and the generic sparse rate sqrt(2 s log(6p / s)) (Lemma 2.4). A matching lower bound on block-equicorrelated designs Z^{(c, k)} with exact RIP constant delta(X, s) = c * sqrt(s - 1) (Lemma 4.1) proves K(X, M_s, alpha, infty) >= A * (c * (s - 1) / sqrt(1 - (s - 1) * c^2)) * sqrt(log floor(k / s)) - sqrt(2 log 2) (Proposition 4.2) and establishes minimax rate optimality whenever delta_p = O(p^{-lambda}) (Corollary 4.3).

native_neighbors.name: Post-model-selection predictor PoSI confidence intervals under full and active-only covariate observation
native_neighbors.definition: A post-model-selection inference methodology for linear regression predictors x_0'[M_hat] beta_hat_{M_hat} +- K(x_0, M_hat) * ||s_{M_hat}|| * sigma_hat (Equation 5), where s_M' = x_0'[M] (X[M]' X[M])^{-1} X[M]' (Equation 6) and bar{s}_M = s_M / ||s_M||, guaranteeing coverage >= 1 - alpha simultaneously over all candidate models M in M_cal and any data-driven model selector M_hat without requiring the true mean mu to be linear. In fixed-design homoscedastic Gaussian regression Y ~ N(mu, sigma^2 I_n) targeting the in-sample optimal linear predictor x_0'[M_hat] beta_{M_hat}^{(n)} with beta_M^{(n)} = (X[M]' X[M])^{-1} X[M]' mu (Equations 3-4, Remark 2.8), observing the full regressor vector x_0 in R^p yields the exact full-information constant K_1(x_0, r), the (1 - alpha)-quantile of max_{M in M_cal} |bar{s}_M' (Y - mu)| / sigma_hat =^d G * max_{M in M_cal} |bar{s}_M' V| (Equation 10, Proposition 2.1, Equation 23). When only the selected covariates x_0[M_hat] are observed at prediction time, K_1(x_0) is infeasible and is replaced by the active-covariate hierarchy K_naive <= K_1(x_0) <= K_2(x_0[M], M) <= K_3(x_0[M], M) <= K_4 <= K_5 (Equations 11-15, Proposition 2.3, Corollary 2.4), where K_2(x_0[M], M) = sup_{x[M] = x_0[M]} K_1(x), K_3(x_0[M], M) is the (1 - alpha)-quantile of the partial spherical-cap union-bound distribution F_{M, x_0}(t) = E_G[1 - min(1, P(max_{M_* subset M} |bar{s}_{M_*}' V| > t/G) + c(M, M_cal) * (1 - F_{Beta, 1/2, (d-1)/2}((t/G)^2)))] separating nested submodels M_* subset M from the c(M, M_cal) non-nested models (Equations 12-14), K_4 = K_3(x_0[emptyset], emptyset) is the full union-bound constant, and K_5 is the Scheffé constant. In random-design regression Y = X beta + U with second-moment matrix Sigma, the same intervals (with either full-model or post-selection variance estimator sigma_hat_{M_hat}^2) asymptotically uniformly cover the design-independent out-of-sample optimal linear predictor x_0'[M_hat] beta_{M_hat}^{(*)} with beta_M^{(*)} = beta[M] + (Sigma[M, M])^{-1} Sigma[M, M^c] beta[M^c] (Section 3, Remark 3.2, Theorem 3.6, Lemma C.2, Theorem D.6).

native_neighbors.name: Uniformly valid post-model-selection confidence intervals via consistent variance overestimation
native_neighbors.definition: A general post-model-selection inference framework and family of confidence intervals CI^{(j)}_{1-alpha, M_hat_n}(y) = theta_hat^{(j)}_{M_hat_n, n}(y) +- sqrt(sigma_hat^2_{rho(M_hat_n)+j, n}(y)) * K_hat_n(y) (Bachoc, Preinerstorfer, & Steinberger 2020, Equation 2.6) for stacked asymptotically linear estimators theta_hat_n(y) - theta^*_n = sum_{i=1}^n g_{i,n}(y_i) + Delta_n(y) in R^k (k = sum_{j=1}^d m(M_{j,n})) satisfying Condition 1, guaranteeing asymptotic coverage liminf_{n -> infty} inf_{P_n in P_n} inf_{M_hat_n} P_n(theta^{*(j)}_{M_hat_n, n} in CI^{(j)}_{1-alpha, M_hat_n}(y)) >= 1 - alpha uniformly over both arbitrary data-driven model selectors M_hat_n and rich classes of possibly misspecified triangular-array distributions P_n (Equations 1.1-1.3, Lemma 2.2, Theorem 2.4, Theorem 2.6). Because uniformly consistent estimation of the true error variance sigma_n^2 is impossible under unbounded model misspecification (Proposition 3.5), the framework replaces consistent variance estimators with consistent variance overestimators nu_hat^2_{j,n}(y) = sum_{i=1}^n [g_tilde^{(j)}_{i,n}(y)]^2 constructed from observable score summands g_tilde^{(j)}_{i,n}(y) = g_hat^{(j)}_{i,n}(y) + a^{(j)}_{i,n} that include unobservable deterministic misspecification shifts a^{(j)}_{i,n}, satisfying P_n(sqrt([V_n(r_n)]_j / nu_hat^2_{j,n}) >= 1 + varepsilon) -> 0 for all misspecification sequences and adapting to exact consistency when misspecification is negligible (Proposition 2.7, Remark 2.8). Paired with either the known-correlation PoSI constants K_{1-alpha}(corr(Gamma_n)) and K_{1-alpha}(corr(Xi_n)) in homoskedastic linear regression (Theorems 3.2-3.3, Proposition 3.4) or the distribution-free rank-adaptive bound B_alpha(rank(Gamma), k) = min_{lambda in (0, 1)} sqrt(q_{1 - lambda*alpha, rank(Gamma)} + 2 log(k / ((1 - lambda)*alpha))) (Lemma 2.9), the framework yields uniformly valid post-selection confidence intervals for heteroskedastic linear regression with Eicker sandwich variances and B_alpha(min(k, p), k) (Theorem 3.6) and for misspecified binary regression with joint link and regressor selection via Fahrmeir quasi-MLE sandwich variances and B_alpha(min(k, n), k) (Theorem 3.11), which reduces to B_alpha(min(k, p), k) under the canonical logistic link (Remark 3.12, Corollary D.3).

native_neighbors.name: Model-robust nonlinearity-consistent sandwich variance and Ratio of Asymptotic Variances (RAV) specification test
native_neighbors.definition: A model-robust theory and diagnostic methodology for ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression under arbitrary joint regressor-response distributions P = P_{Y, X_vec} without assuming linearity or homoskedasticity (Buja, Berk, Brown, George, Pitkin, Traskin, Zhao, & Zhang 2019). Viewing the population OLS parameter beta(P) = E[X_vec X_vec']^{-1} E[X_vec Y] = E[X_vec X_vec']^{-1} E[X_vec mu(X_vec)] (Equations 3-4) as a statistical functional of the joint distribution P, Proposition 4.1 proves that regressor ancillarity fails whenever the conditional mean mu(x_vec) = E[Y | X_vec = x_vec] is nonlinear because beta(P) then depends on the marginal regressor distribution P_{X_vec}. Decomposing the response as Y = beta' X_vec + eta(X_vec) + eps with canonical nonlinearity eta(X_vec) = mu(X_vec) - beta' X_vec and noise eps = Y - mu(X_vec) satisfying E[X_vec eta(X_vec)] = 0, E[X_vec eps] = 0, E[eta(X_vec) eps] = 0, and conditional MSE m^2(X_vec) = sigma^2(X_vec) + eta^2(X_vec) (Section 5, Equations 6-9), the framework separates the Total Estimation Offset beta_hat - beta(P) into the uncorrelated Noise Estimation Offset beta_hat - beta(X) and Approximation Estimation Offset beta(X) - beta(P), where beta(X) = (X'X)^{-1} X' mu(X) is the conditional target of fixed-X regression (Equations 10-15), both of order O_P(N^{-1/2}) with asymptotic covariance matrices E[X_vec X_vec']^{-1} E[sigma^2(X_vec) X_vec X_vec'] E[X_vec X_vec']^{-1} and E[X_vec X_vec']^{-1} E[eta^2(X_vec) X_vec X_vec'] E[X_vec X_vec']^{-1} whose sum is consistently estimated by the Eicker-Huber-White sandwich estimator AV_hat_sand[beta] = lim_{M -> infty} M V_{P_hat_N}[beta^*_M] (Propositions 7, 8.1, 8.2, Equations 16-20). Using adjusted regressors X_{j.} = X_j - beta_{-j}' X_vec_{-j}, the j-th slope admits case-wise and pairwise weighted-average representations (Section 10, Equations 22-23), and the Ratio of Asymptotic Variances RAV[beta_j, m^2] = AV_total[beta_j] / AV_lin[beta_j] = E[m^2(X_vec) X_{j.}^2] / (E[m^2(X_vec)] E[X_{j.}^2]) = w_sigma RAV[beta_j, sigma^2] + w_eta RAV[beta_j, eta^2] (Definition 11.4, Lemma E.2, Equation 27) quantifies regressor-specific protective (RAV < 1) vs. anti-protective (RAV > 1) standard-error distortion within sharp range [P-min X_{j.}^2 / E[X_{j.}^2], P-max X_{j.}^2 / E[X_{j.}^2]] (Proposition 11.5) and yields the regressor-specific test statistic RAV_hat_j = N <r^2, X_{j,.hat}^2> / (||r||^2 ||X_{j,.hat}||^2) with asymptotic null variance (E[delta^4]/E[delta^2]^2)(E[X_{j.}^4]/E[X_{j.}^2]^2) - 1 (Proposition 12.2, Equation 30) and a permutation test (Section 12.3).

native_neighbors.name: Model-free regression functionals, regressor-reweighting well-specification diagnostic, and M-of-N XY-bootstrap sandwich limit
native_neighbors.definition: A general model-free theory and diagnostic framework for parametric and penalized regression estimators viewed as statistical functionals theta(P) of the joint response-regressor distribution P = P_{Y|X_vec} (x) P_{X_vec} on arbitrary measurable spaces (Buja, Brown, Kuchibhotla, Berk, George, & Zhao 2019). Encompassing optimization functionals theta(P) = argmin_theta E_P[L(theta; Y, X_vec)] (including maximum likelihood KL-divergence functionals, proper scoring rule Bregman-divergence functionals such as the Basu-Harris-Hjort-Jones density power divergence S_alpha with Fisher consistency and redescending influence functions for alpha > 0, and penalized functionals) and estimating-equation (EE) functionals solving E_P[psi(theta; Y, X_vec)] = 0 (Section 2, Equations 1-7, Appendix A.2), the framework defines theta(.) to be well-specified for P_{Y|X_vec} iff theta(P_{Y|X_vec} (x) P_{X_vec}) = theta(P_{Y|X_vec} (x) P'_{X_vec}) for all acceptable regressor distributions P_{X_vec}, P'_{X_vec} (Section 3.1, Propositions 3.3.1-3.3.3). Because regressor-only reweighting P^w(dy, dx_vec) = w(x_vec) P(dy, dx_vec) with E_P[w(X_vec)] = 1 preserves P^w_{Y|X_vec} = P_{Y|X_vec} (Lemma 4.1), any well-specified functional satisfies theta(P^w) = theta(P) (Proposition 4.1), motivating the one-parameter Gaussian reweighting diagnostic trace xi |-> theta_hat_xi = theta(w_hat_xi(Z) P_hat) across interior deciles xi_(1) < ... < xi_(K) of a reweighting variable Z = f(X_vec) and the two-point bootstrap tilt test statistic d = theta_hat_{xi_(K)} - theta_hat_{xi_(1)} (Sections 4-5, Equations 8-9). Conditioning on the empirical regressor distribution P_hat_{X_vec} defines the conditional parameter theta(X) = theta(P_{Y|X_vec} (x) P_hat_{X_vec}) and decomposes the Total Estimation Offset theta_hat - theta(P) into the Noise Estimation Offset theta_hat - theta(X) and Approximation Estimation Offset theta(X) - theta(P) (Section 6, Propositions 6.4-6.5), governed by the full influence function IF(Y, X_vec) and partial influence function IF(x_vec) = E_P[IF(Y, X_vec) | X_vec = x_vec] (Equations 10-11, Lemma 6.6), which vanishes iff theta(.) is well-specified (Proposition 6.6) and yields the orthogonal Pythagorean CLT variance split V_P[IF(Y, X_vec)] = E_P[V_P[IF(Y, X_vec) | X_vec]] + V_P[IF(X_vec)] (Section 7, Corollary 7.1) and the exact M-of-N XY-bootstrap sandwich limit M^{1/2}(theta^*_M - theta_hat_N) ->^D N(0, AV[P_hat_N; theta(.)]) as M -> infty for fixed N (Section 8, Proposition 8.1, Corollary 8.1).

native_neighbors.name: Unified assumption-lean moving-target linear regression and score bootstrap
native_neighbors.definition: An assumption-lean statistical estimation and inference methodology for ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression that starts with the empirical OLS estimator beta_hat_n = Sigma_hat_n^{-1} Gamma_hat_n (where Sigma_hat_n := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n X_i X_i^T and Gamma_hat_n := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n X_i Y_i) and defines its sample-size-dependent moving target of estimation beta_n := Sigma_n^{-1} Gamma_n = argmin_{theta in R^p} 1/n sum_{i=1}^n E[(Y_i - X_i^T theta)^2] (where Sigma_n := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i X_i^T] and Gamma_n := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i Y_i]; Definition 2.1, Equations 9-14) across a unified framework of independent, possibly non-identically distributed (i.n.i.d.) observation vectors (X_i^T, Y_i)^T in R^{p+1} encompassing both fixed covariates and random covariates (Kuchibhotla, Brown, & Buja 2018). Because the population normal equation 1/n sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i(Y_i - X_i^T beta_n)] = 0 holds on average while individual score expectations E[X_i(Y_i - X_i^T beta_n)] are generally non-zero under fixed or non-identically distributed covariates with nonlinearity, the centered score vectors S_i := X_i(Y_i - X_i^T beta_n) - E[X_i(Y_i - X_i^T beta_n)] have true covariance K_n = 1/n sum_{i=1}^n E[S_i S_i^T] satisfying Bentkus's multidimensional Berry-Esseen bound over convex sets C_p subseteq R^p (Theorem 2.1, Theorem 5.1, Equations 16-17), while the uncentered second-moment matrix K_n^* := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i X_i^T (Y_i - X_i^T beta_n)^2] dominates K_n in Loewner order (K_n <= K_n^*). Pairing the empirical plug-in matrix K_check_n := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n X_i X_i^T (Y_i - X_i^T beta_hat_n)^2 with Anderson's (1955) Lemma (Lemma 6.2), the methodology constructs asymptotically conservative confidence regions and simultaneous tests via the Eicker-Huber-White sandwich estimator Sigma_hat_n^{-1} K_check_n Sigma_hat_n^{-1} (Equation 18) and matrix-inversion-free multiplier and m-of-n resampling score bootstraps on the estimated score vectors S_hat_i := X_i(Y_i - X_i^T beta_hat_n) (Sections 6.2-7, Equations 20-29), backed by an assumption-free deterministic master inequality (Theorem 8.1, Equations 30-32) and semiparametric efficiency of beta_hat_n for beta_n (Appendix A, Lemma A.1, Equations 33-36).

native_neighbors.name: Simultaneous normal-equation post-selection confidence regions in model-free linear regression
native_neighbors.definition: Simultaneous normal-equation post-selection confidence regions in model-free linear regression are an assumption-lean statistical inference methodology introduced by Kuchibhotla, Brown, Buja, Cai, George, and Zhao (2020, The Annals of Statistics 48(5):2953-2981, arXiv:1806.04119v1, DOI:10.1214/19-AOS1917) for constructing universally valid post-selection confidence regions across arbitrary data-dependent submodel selectors M_hat in M_p subseteq M_p(p) := {M subseteq {1,...,p} : 1 <= |M| <= p} for independent (possibly non-identically distributed) or functionally dependent observations (X_i^T, Y_i)^T in R^p x R. For each submodel M, the submodel ordinary least squares estimator beta_hat_{n,M} and the model-free submodel moving target beta_{n,M} solve the submodel normal equations Sigma_hat_n(M) beta_hat_{n,M} = Gamma_hat_n(M) and Sigma_n(M) beta_{n,M} = Gamma_n(M), where Sigma_hat_n := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n X_i X_i^T, Gamma_hat_n := 1/n sum_{i=1}^n X_i Y_i, Sigma_n := E[Sigma_hat_n], and Gamma_n := E[Gamma_hat_n] (Section 2.2, Equations 4-6). After proving that universal post-selection validity P(beta_{n,M_hat} in R_hat_{n,M_hat}) >= 1 - alpha over all selectors M_hat with P(M_hat in M_p) = 1 is strictly equivalent to simultaneous family-wise validity P(bigcap_{M in M_p} {beta_{n,M} in R_hat_{n,M}}) >= 1 - alpha (Section 3, Theorem 3.1, Equation 9), the method exploits the assumption-free deterministic normal-equation inequality ||Sigma_hat_n(M) {beta_{n,M} - beta_hat_{n,M}}||_infty <= D_n^Gamma + D_n^Sigma ||beta_{n,M}||_1 for all M in M_p(p) (Equations 17-18), where D_n^Sigma := |||Sigma_hat_n - Sigma_n|||_infty = max_{M in M_p(2)} |||Sigma_hat_n(M) - Sigma_n(M)|||_infty and D_n^Gamma := ||Gamma_hat_n - Gamma_n||_infty = max_{M in M_p(1)} ||Gamma_hat_n(M) - Gamma_n(M)||_infty depend only on marginal and bivariate moments (Equation 12). Using bivariate joint (1-alpha)-quantiles (C_n^Gamma(alpha), C_n^Sigma(alpha)) of (D_n^Gamma, D_n^Sigma) estimated in polynomial O(n p^2) time via a high-dimensional Gaussian multiplier bootstrap on the q = p + p(p+1)/2 unique cross-product and Gram coordinates W_i = ({X_i(j) Y_i}, {X_i(l) X_i(m)}_{l <= m}) (Section 5, Theorem 5.1), the method defines the exact finite-sample simultaneous confidence region R_hat_{n,M} := {theta in R^{|M|} : ||Sigma_hat_n(M)(beta_hat_{n,M} - theta)||_infty <= C_n^Gamma(alpha) + C_n^Sigma(alpha) ||theta||_1} (Equation 13, Theorem 4.1) and its asymptotically valid 2|M|-constraint parallelepiped approximation R_hat_{n,M}^dagger := {theta in R^{|M|} : ||Sigma_hat_n(M)(beta_hat_{n,M} - theta)||_infty <= C_n^Gamma(alpha) + C_n^Sigma(alpha) ||beta_hat_{n,M}||_1} (Equation 14, Theorem 4.2), whose Lebesgue volume O_p(sqrt(|M| log(p)/n))^{|M|} adapts to the selected model cardinality |M| rather than the maximum search size k (Proposition 4.1, Equations 21 and 28).

native_neighbors.name: Generalized Bernstein-Orlicz sub-Weibull concentration and high-dimensional misspecified Lasso
native_neighbors.definition: Generalized Bernstein-Orlicz sub-Weibull concentration and high-dimensional misspecified Lasso is a non-asymptotic heavy-tailed probability and high-dimensional statistical estimation methodology introduced by Kuchibhotla and Chakrabortty (2022, Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA 11(4):1389-1456, arXiv:1804.02605v4, DOI:10.1093/imaiai/iaac012). It unifies sub-Gaussian (alpha = 2), sub-exponential (alpha = 1), and heavy-tailed Weibull-type (alpha > 0, including non-convex Orlicz regimes alpha < 1 where moment-generating functions need not exist) random variables via the sub-Weibull(alpha) Orlicz quasi-norm ||X||_{psi_alpha} := inf{eta > 0 : E[psi_alpha(|X|/eta)] <= 1} with psi_alpha(x) = exp(x^alpha) - 1 (Definitions 2.1-2.2), and introduces the Generalized Bernstein-Orlicz (GBO) quasi-norm ||X||_{Psi_{alpha,L}} := inf{eta > 0 : E[Psi_{alpha,L}(|X|/eta)] <= 1} defined by its inverse function Psi_{alpha,L}^{-1}(t) := sqrt(log(1 + t)) + L(log(1 + t))^{1/alpha} for alpha > 0, L >= 0 (Definition 2.3, Equation 2.5). The GBO norm is equivalent up to factor 2 to the closed-form two-regime Orlicz quasi-norm ||X||_{phi_{alpha,L}} with phi_{alpha,L}(x) = exp(min{x^2, (x/L)^alpha}) - 1 (Proposition A.1), yields the sharp two-regime Gaussian-plus-Weibull tail inequality P(|X| >= ||X||_{Psi_{alpha,L}}{sqrt(t) + L t^{1/alpha}}) <= 2 exp(-t) (Proposition A.3), satisfies Latala-type and Adamczak-Hoffmann-Jorgensen variance-scaling concentration bounds for sums of independent random variables (Theorems 3.1-3.3) and high-dimensional maxima improving Chernozhukov-Chetverikov-Kato (Theorem 3.4, Remark 3.2), obeys a Holder-type product Orlicz inequality ||prod_{i=1}^k W_i||_{psi_beta} <= prod_{i=1}^k ||W_i||_{psi_{alpha_i}} for 1/beta = sum_{i=1}^k 1/alpha_i (Proposition D.2), extends to suprema of unbounded empirical processes with sub-Weibull envelopes (Theorem B.1), and formally separates marginal sub-Weibull tails ||X||_{M,psi_alpha} := max_{1<=j<=q} ||X(j)||_{psi_alpha} from joint sub-Weibull tails ||X||_{J,psi_alpha} := sup_{||theta||_2=1} ||X^T theta||_{psi_alpha} (Definitions 2.4-2.5) to establish non-asymptotic rates for elementwise covariance estimation (Theorems 4.1-4.2), k-sparse operator norm RIP_n(k) (Theorem 4.3), unified Restricted Strong Convexity (RSC) and free-sparsity s-optimized Restricted Eigenvalue RE(k) sample complexity (Theorem 4.4, Section 4.3.1), and hard-sparsity-free oracle inequalities for high-dimensional misspecified Lasso under sub-Weibull or polynomial-tailed errors (Theorems 4.5-4.6, Proposition E.1).

native_neighbors.name: Uniform-in-submodel deterministic linear regression and functional dependence bounds
native_neighbors.definition: Uniform-in-submodel deterministic linear regression and functional dependence bounds are a model-free high-dimensional statistical methodology introduced by Kuchibhotla, Brown, Buja, George, and Zhao (2021, arXiv:1802.05801v3) for simultaneously controlling estimation error and first-order Bahadur linear representation remainders across all covariate subsets M in M(k) := {M subseteq {1,...,p} : 1 <= |M| <= k}. Defining the general linear regression map beta_M(Sigma, Gamma) := [Sigma(M)]^{-1} Gamma(M) for any symmetric positive-definite p x p matrix Sigma and p-vector Gamma (encompassing ordinary least squares, Catoni/Minsker heavy-tailed Gram estimators, outlier-robust estimators, and Loh-Wainwright noisy or missing-data surrogate estimators, Section 3.3), the framework introduces the k-sparse submatrix operator norm RIP(k, Sigma_1 - Sigma_2) := sup_{M in M(k)} ||Sigma_1(M) - Sigma_2(M)||_{op}, the k-sparse vector norm D(k, Gamma_1 - Gamma_2) := sup_{M in M(k)} ||Gamma_1(M) - Gamma_2(M)||_2, and the k-sparse minimum eigenvalue Lambda(k; Sigma_2) := inf_{||theta||_0<=k} ||Sigma_2 theta||_2 / ||theta||_2 (Equations 13-14). Whenever RIP(k, Sigma_1 - Sigma_2) < Lambda(k; Sigma_2), Theorem 1 proves the assumption-free deterministic uniform l2 bound ||beta_M(Sigma_1, Gamma_1) - beta_M(Sigma_2, Gamma_2)||_2 <= [D(k, Gamma_1 - Gamma_2) + RIP(k, Sigma_1 - Sigma_2) ||beta_M(Sigma_2, Gamma_2)||_2] / [Lambda(k; Sigma_2) - RIP(k, Sigma_1 - Sigma_2)] simultaneously for all M in M(k), and Theorem 3 proves the deterministic uniform Bahadur linear representation bound ||beta_M(Sigma_1, Gamma_1) - beta_M(Sigma_2, Gamma_2) - [Sigma_2(M)]^{-1}{Gamma_1(M) - Sigma_1(M) beta_M(Sigma_2, Gamma_2)}||_2 <= [RIP(k, Sigma_1 - Sigma_2) / Lambda(k; Sigma_2)] ||beta_M(Sigma_1, Gamma_1) - beta_M(Sigma_2, Gamma_2)||_2 with matching two-sided sandwiching (Remarks 3.2-3.3). Combining these deterministic inequalities with epsilon-net covering of Theta_k (Section 4) and a dyadic martingale plus blocking decomposition under Wu's (2005) functional dependence measure with dependence-adjusted sub-Weibull norms ||{W}||_{psi_alpha,nu} (Section 5, Theorem 12) yields uniform O_p(sqrt(k log(ep/k)/n)) consistency and O_p(k log(ep/k)/n) linear representation remainders for independent and causal time-series data.

native_neighbors.name: Deterministic Banach contraction and Newton-Kantorovich inequalities for smooth M-estimators
native_neighbors.definition: Deterministic Banach contraction and Newton-Kantorovich inequalities for smooth M-estimators are a finite-sample, assumption-free analytical framework introduced by Kuchibhotla (2018, arXiv:1809.05172v1) that decouples the existence, localization, and first-order Bahadur influence-function expansion of zeros of smooth estimating equations f(theta) = 0 from any probabilistic or i.i.d. data-generating assumptions. Using the Banach fixed-point theorem applied to phi(theta) := theta - A^{-1} f(theta) on B(theta_0, r), Theorem 2.1 proves that whenever sup_{theta in B(theta_0, r)} ||A^{-1}(A - nabla f(theta))||_{op} <= varepsilon < 1 and ||A^{-1} f(theta_0)||_2 <= r(1 - varepsilon) for an arbitrary reference point theta_0 (not necessarily satisfying E[f(theta_0)] = 0), there exists a unique root theta^* in B(theta_0, r) satisfying the two-sided norm sandwiching (1 + varepsilon)^{-1} ||A^{-1} f(theta_0)||_2 <= ||theta^* - theta_0||_2 <= (1 - varepsilon)^{-1} ||A^{-1} f(theta_0)||_2; under local Holder Jacobian continuity ||[nabla f(theta_0)]^{-1}(nabla f(theta_0) - nabla f(theta))||_{op} <= L ||theta - theta_0||_2^alpha, Theorem 2.2 establishes the semilocal Newton-Kantorovich Bahadur expansion ||theta^* - theta_0 + [nabla f(theta_0)]^{-1} f(theta_0)||_2 <= (1.5)^{1+alpha} L ||[nabla f(theta_0)]^{-1} f(theta_0)||_2^{1+alpha}. For smooth convex losses L(theta; w), Section 3 introduces the scale-invariant directional Hessian-ratio modulus C(u, w) := sup_{||theta_1 - theta_2||_2 <= u} sup_{||e||_2 = 1} (e^T nabla_2 L(theta_1, w) e) / (e^T nabla_2 L(theta_2, w) e) >= 1 (forming a convex cone C_T under nonnegative combinations, Proposition 3.1) and proves in Theorem 3.1 that whenever max_{1<=i<=n} C(delta_n(theta_0), W_i) <= 4/3 with delta_n(theta_0) := 1.5 ||[Q_hat_n(theta_0)]^{-1} Z_hat_n(theta_0)||_2, a root theta_hat_n exists with (1/2) delta_n(theta_0) <= ||theta_hat_n - theta_0||_2 <= delta_n(theta_0) and ||theta_hat_n - theta_0 + [Q_hat_n(theta_0)]^{-1} Z_hat_n(theta_0)||_2 <= max_{1<=i<=n} {C(delta_n(theta_0), W_i) - 1} delta_n(theta_0), extending directly to generalized linear models (Corollary 3.1), Cox proportional hazards partial likelihood (Theorem 4.1), non-convex least squares (Corollary 5.1), equality-constrained KKT systems (Corollary 6.1), and sample-computable leave-k-out cross-validation, marginal screening, and uniform-in-submodel post-selection inference (Corollaries 7.1-7.4).

native_neighbors.name: OLS post-Lasso and fitness-thresholded post-model selection estimation
native_neighbors.definition: OLS post-Lasso and fitness-thresholded post-model selection estimation are a nonasymptotic two-step high-dimensional nonparametric regression methodology introduced by Belloni and Chernozhukov (2013, Bernoulli 19(2):521-547, arXiv:1001.0188v5, DOI:10.3150/11-BEJ410) that applies ordinary least squares (OLS) to the covariate support T_hat(t) := support(beta_hat(t)) selected by a first-step L1-penalized Lasso estimator beta_hat in argmin_beta {Q_hat(beta) + (lambda/n)||beta||_1} with data-driven noise-gradient quantile penalty lambda = c' sigma_hat Lambda(1 - alpha | X) (Equation 2.12). Benchmarking against the oracle risk minimization program min_{0<=k<=p^n} (c_k^2 + sigma^2 k / n) with oracle target beta_0, support T (|T| = s), and approximation error c_s^2 = E_n[(f_. - x_.' beta_0)^2] (Equations 2.2-2.4), Section 3.3 combines empirical presparsity (Lemma 2) with the sublinearity of restricted sparse eigenvalues phi(ceil(ell k)) <= ceil(ell) phi(k) (Lemma 3) to prove the sharp false-positive sparsity bound m_hat := |T_hat \ T| <= s [min_{m in M} phi(m ^ n)] L_n = O_P(s) (Theorem 3). For any generic first-step selector T_hat, Theorem 4 proves via Samorodnitsky-Talagrand empirical process control (Lemmas 4-5) that the post-selection OLS estimator beta_tilde in argmin_{beta_{T_hat^c}=0} Q_hat(beta) satisfies ||f_tilde - f||_{P_n,2} <= K_varepsilon sigma sqrt((m_hat log p + (m_hat + s) log(e mu(m_hat))) / n) + 3 c_s + sqrt((B_n)_+ ^ (C_n)_+) where B_n := Q_hat(beta_hat) - Q_hat(beta_0) and C_n := Q_hat(beta_{0 T_hat}) - Q_hat(beta_0), establishing that OLS post-Lasso (t = 0) and OLS post-fit Lasso (with data-driven goodness-of-fit threshold t_gamma := max{t >= 0 : Q_hat(beta_tilde^t) - Q_hat(beta_hat) <= gamma}, gamma <= 0, Equations 2.9 and 2.14) achieve the near-oracle rate O_P(sigma sqrt(s log p / n) + c_s) even when model selection misses true components (T not subseteq T_hat) and achieve strictly faster rates than Lasso (down to the exact oracle rate O_P(sigma sqrt(s/n) + c_s)) when T subseteq T_hat and m_hat = o_P(s) (Theorems 5-6, Corollaries 2-3).

native_neighbors.definition: Self-Concordant and Pseudo-Self-Concordant Finite-Sample M-Estimation is a non-asymptotic statistical estimation and excess-risk analysis methodology for empirical risk minimizers (ERM) theta_hat_n in Argmin_{theta in Theta} L_n(theta) and l_1-penalized M-estimators theta_hat_{lambda,n} in Argmin_{theta in R^d} {L_n(theta) + lambda ||theta||_1} in random-design linear prediction models ell_Z(theta) = ell(Y, X^T theta) that characterizes the critical sample size n needed to achieve the Wilks-Fisher chi-square-type excess risk bound L(theta_hat_n) - L(theta_*) <= C K_1^2 d_eff log(e/delta) / n where d_eff = Tr(H^{-1/2} G H^{-1/2}) is the effective dimension, H = nabla^2 L(theta_*) = E[ell''(Y, X^T theta_*) X X^T], and G = E[nabla ell_Z(theta_*) nabla ell_Z(theta_*)^T]. By exploiting either pseudo-self-concordance (|ell'''(y, eta)| <= ell''(y, eta), Assumption SCa) or canonical self-concordance (|ell'''(y, eta)| <= 2 [ell''(y, eta)]^{3/2}, Assumption SCb, including novel Fenchel-conjugate canonically self-concordant pseudo-Huber and classification surrogate losses) together with local sub-Gaussian calibrated-design assumptions at theta_* or over the population Dikin ellipsoid Theta_r(theta_*) = {theta in R^d : ||theta - theta_*||_{H(theta_*)} <= r}, the methodology localizes theta_hat_n without global empirical-process chaining and establishes critical sample sizes O(rho d d_eff) or O(d d_eff) under pointwise local assumptions at theta_* and near-linear critical sample sizes O(max{rho d_eff, d log d}) or O(max{d_eff, d log d}) via an epsilon-net covering argument over the Dikin ellipsoid.

additional_rows.name: INLA group node conflict diagnostic
additional_rows.definition: A group-wise Bayesian model diagnostic for latent Gaussian models that uses two INLA fits per selected group to compare remaining-data and within-group information about its latent linear predictor vector. Fitted mean and covariance summaries yield a quadratic conflict score with a rank-based Gaussian chi-square reference. Nuisance-parameter updating, replication dependence and numerical rank choices determine the interpretation.
